subtopic: Drawn into a high-control group or online extremism
passage:
Jahnavi, you asked why I'm always on my phone now. Okay. Since Papa moved to the Gulf for work, the house is so quiet. Mummy works late. And after I got 48 in the prelims, nobody at school really talks to me except to ask my marks.
Then in the game forum I met this group. Older, maybe eighteen, twenty. They're so nice, Jahnavi. When I said I was stressed, one of them sent me a long message about how exams don't define you. They ask how my day was. Every day. They remember my cat's name.
Last night I couldn't sleep, and at two in the morning someone was still there, talking to me about music. They said, 'You're one of us now, Akash.'
Nobody's asked me for anything. They just, I don't know, get me.
Why are you making that face?

qa.q: What mark did Akash get in the prelims?
What is Akash feeling that makes the group feel so good?
qa.a: Akash feels lonely at home and unseen at school, so the group's attention feels like finally being understood.

qa.q: What turning point is available now, before the group asks for anything?
qa.a: Akash could tell Mummy or a school counsellor about the new online group and about feeling lonely, and keep up real-life friendships like Jahnavi's.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi be worried about while listening?
qa.a: Jahnavi may worry that strangers online are giving so much attention so fast, and that Akash is relying on them more than on people nearby.

grounding: It shows a lonely teen, strained by exams and a parent away, drawn to an online group that meets real needs with warmth before any demands.

I'm Devika, Wasim's cousin. I stayed with his family for the summer, so I can only say what I saw.
Wasim failed his Class 10 maths in May. His parents were fighting a lot then, doors banging. He spent most days in his room.
In June he started going to something he called 'the youth circle', in a rented hall near the bus depot. Two older boys came on a motorbike to pick him up. They brought him back late, with samosas for everyone, and called my aunt 'Aunty-ji' very politely.
Wasim smiled more. He started ironing his shirts. Once I heard him on the phone saying, 'They actually listen, yaar.'
When I asked what they did there, he said, 'Nothing, we just talk. They say I'm family now.'
Nobody had asked him for money or anything. I don't know what's going on in his head. But he'd never had that many phone calls before.

qa.q: Where was the rented hall for 'the youth circle'?
qa.a: It was in a rented hall near the bus depot.

qa.q: What might Wasim be feeling that makes the circle so appealing?
qa.a: He seems lonely and low after failing maths and hearing his parents fight, so being listened to and called family feels like a relief.

qa.q: What could Devika or Wasim's parents do at this early stage?
qa.a: They could spend real time with Wasim, ask openly and calmly about the circle, and talk to a trusted adult such as a school counsellor if anything worries them.

qa.q: How does Devika see the change in Wasim, and why is Devika unsure about it?
qa.a: Devika sees him happier and busier, but can't tell what is behind it, and the sudden warmth from older strangers makes Devika uneasy.

grounding: It shows, through a cousin's eyes, a lonely teen strained by exam failure and family conflict being drawn into a warm group that meets his needs before any demands.
